nodes.label: Matthew Frye Jacobson
nodes.date_label: Whiteness of a Different Color (1998) · Barbarian Virtues (2000) · Roots Too (2006)
nodes.description: A historian of race, migration and political culture in the United States. His written PBS interview explains how distinctions among European immigrants were once treated as racial differences and later reconfigured as ethnicity. He connects those changing categories to arguments about fitness for citizenship and self-government. The entry treats racial classifications as historical objects, retains the distinctions between scholarly claims and the categories of historical actors, and does not certify every example in the unread monographs.

nodes.label: Roy Porter

The entry also preserves his co-editorship of a major consumption collection without assigning its contributors’ arguments to him.

nodes.label: Lawrence Stone
nodes.date_label: The Crisis of the Aristocracy (1965) · The Family, Sex and Marriage in England (1977) · The Family, Sex and Marriage: abridged edition (1979) · “The Revival of Narrative” (1979)

nodes.label: Philip J Deloria
nodes.date_label: Playing Indian (1998) · Indians in Unexpected Places (2004) · Becoming Mary Sully: Toward an American Indian Abstract (2019)
nodes.description: A historian of American Indian peoples, representation and modernity. The same account explains how family preservation, research, public talks and curatorial questions helped turn overlooked drawings into a historical argument and exhibitions; that collaboration does not make him the artwork’s author.

nodes.label: Linda K Kerber
nodes.date_label: Women of the Republic (1980) · “Separate Spheres, Female Worlds, Woman’s Place” (1988) · No Constitutional Right to Be Ladies (1998)
nodes.description: A historian of women, political ideas and citizenship in the United States. Her 1988 essay examines how a language used by historical actors became an interpretive device for historians: separate spheres can conceal changing relationships when treated as a fixed social map. In her published 2001 lecture she investigates how apparently protective exemptions and unequal obligations helped structure gendered citizenship. The entry keeps this historical analysis distinct from current legal advice and from claiming one uniform experience for all women.

nodes.label: John Lewis Gaddis
nodes.date_label: Strategies of Containment (1982) · We Now Know: Rethinking Cold War History (1997) · The Landscape of History (2002)
nodes.description: A historian of the Cold War and strategy whose selected writings revisit historical explanations as evidence and perspectives change. In a 1998 primary essay he connects the opening of former communist archives with revisions to Cold War interpretation, while admitting that no historical representation can recover everything. He argues for greater attention to ideology and offers a separate, controversial account of nuclear weapons as both stabilizing and prolonging the conflict. Those are Gaddis’s interpretations, not settled judgments about comparative regimes or the whole Cold War.

nodes.label: François Furet
nodes.date_label: “Le Catéchisme révolutionnaire” (1971) · Penser la Révolution française (1978) · Interpreting the French Revolution: Elborg Forster translation (1981) · Le Passé d’une illusion (1995)
nodes.description: A historian of the French Revolution and political ideas whose work challenged an established social interpretation of revolution. In the opening of his 1971 essay he attacks what he calls a Jacobin historiography, distinguishing its commemorative commitments from critical inquiry. Gérard Grunberg’s substantive 1979 reading identifies a further argument about political language and the representation of popular sovereignty. Both the polemic and its later interpretation remain attributed; the entry does not endorse either a general verdict on Marx or an inevitable path from 1789 to twentieth-century regimes.

nodes.scope_note: New identity matched to the French-Revolution historian and BnF/Académie records. Argument support is the bounded original essay and Grunberg’s expressly named reading. Furet/Richet coauthorship of earlier work remains distinct; no group work is reassigned. Original essay, revised collection, translation and later monograph stay separate. His criticism targets a particular historical interpretation, not a personal causal influence or blanket theory classification.

edges.relationship: Historicizes shifting racial subdivisions within whiteness and their reconfiguration as ethnic differences.
edges.evidence_note: Primary written interview, opening questions on race around 1900 and immigration. These are the historian’s arguments about changing classifications; quoted historical categories are not endorsed.

edges.relationship: Connects racial classification with historical disputes about naturalization and fitness for self-government.
edges.evidence_note: Primary answer on immigration and the 1790 naturalization framework, plus the discussion of later immigration debates. This is a particular historical interpretation, not current legal guidance or an influence arrow.

edges.relationship: Investigates lay interpretation, domestic treatment and the sufferer’s role in medical encounters.
edges.evidence_note: Existing primary opening of Lay Medical Knowledge, supplemented by the publisher’s displayed conclusion of The Patient’s View. Claims are bounded to these passages, not autonomous or equally documented agency for all patients.

edges.relationship: Moves the historical gaze toward sickness, self-help and community healing as problems of social history.
edges.evidence_note: Displayed primary conclusion explicitly connects health and social history and declines premature uniform interaction models. Full article unread. No general claim that professionals were absent or powerless in every context.

edges.relationship: Interprets enslaved culture and paternalism as contested forms within a system of domination.
edges.evidence_note: Existing complete preface and initial paternalism paragraphs, plus Walter Johnson’s complete retrospective, within their recorded scopes. Paternalism is not a benign-slavery claim; Johnson’s consent/coercion criticism remains visible.

edges.relationship: Makes the relation between slaveholding class power, economic organization and development a problem for Marxist historical interpretation.
edges.evidence_note: Specific political-economy intervention mediated by N. Gordon Levin’s substantive review, selected opening pages. This is a contribution to a contested interpretation, not proof that every Marxist shared it, or a direct personal influence from Marx or Gramsci.

edges.relationship: Offers a qualified interpretation of family change and affective relations whose evidential assumptions Pollock disputes.
edges.evidence_note: Primary abridgment pp. 21–29 and Pollock’s separate 1981 thesis passages, within existing scopes. Stone acknowledges literate-source bias while assuming broad representativeness; neither his trajectory nor that assumption is certified.

edges.relationship: Diagnoses renewed narrative among a prominent minority while acknowledging continuing quantitative and analytical work.
edges.evidence_note: Existing primary Stone reading covers pp. 3–6 and 13–24, not 7–12; Hobsbawm response read completely. Diagnosis and examples remain Stone’s situated claims, not a unanimous field transition.

edges.relationship: Examines how a chosen historical inquiry organizes events and explanations without making their relations arbitrary.
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary extract, opening on event relevance and the sections on intrigue and the event field. Bernard Dantier’s introductory commentary is separately attributed and not treated as Veyne’s text.

edges.relationship: Provides a comparison with the later narrative debate: Veyne’s intrigue can connect temporal rhythms without requiring a chronological storyline.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit editorial methodological comparison between the selected 1971 extract and the bounded 1979 Stone reading. No influence, direct exchange or Veyne affiliation with a narrative movement is asserted.

edges.relationship: Challenges a categorical boundary between Indigenous life and modernity through the case of Mary Sully’s art.
edges.evidence_note: Primary written answer on being native to modernism, 2024. The argument concerns a distinctive artist and does not make her representative of all Indigenous people. The complete book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Explains a collaborative route from family-held drawings through historical research and public talks to museum interpretation.
edges.evidence_note: Primary Q&A answers on rediscovery, curatorial challenges, book formation and exhibitions. Deloria credits his mother, audiences and named curators; this records historical/public interpretation, not sole creation of the art or a generic museum affiliation.

edges.relationship: Examines how the separate-spheres metaphor shaped both historical prescriptions and historians’ accounts of women.
edges.evidence_note: Primary printed pp. 9–11 and 38–39 read. The critique treats the metaphor as a historically located interpretive problem, not proof that women never faced exclusions or that spaces were never gendered.

edges.relationship: Investigates gendered citizenship through unequal civic burdens, exemptions and authority.
edges.evidence_note: Primary Kerber section of the Summer 2001 Bulletin talk, opening and the Reed/citizenship discussion. Robert Post’s separate introduction is not attributed to her. Historical legal examples are her account, not current-law certification.

edges.relationship: Reassesses Cold War political power through ideology, legitimacy and newly available evidence.
edges.evidence_note: Primary essay’s opening and second numbered argument, read. His comparative claims about regime performance and Soviet legitimacy remain attributed and disputable. This does not treat access to some archives as complete evidence.

edges.relationship: Argues that nuclear deterrence could both stabilize crises and prolong the Cold War by masking other dimensions of state power.
edges.evidence_note: Primary essay’s third argument explicitly distinguishes these two effects. It is a contested historical interpretation, not a generic military appointment arrow or a validated counterfactual for every crisis.

edges.relationship: Makes source criticism and estimation central to reconstructing the scale of the Atlantic slave trade.
edges.evidence_note: Named substantive reader Joseph C. Miller’s 2009 account of the census’s origin, uncertainty and later archival responses. No fresh reading of the census or audit of modern SlaveVoyages totals; counting is not a substitute for enslaved experience.

edges.relationship: Develops comparative questions around recurring cross-cultural trade, migration, plantations and disease.
edges.evidence_note: Miller’s substantive account supplies the methodological characterization; the publisher record supports title/date only. A specific comparative agenda, not the claim that one historian founded all global history or a causal affiliation arrow.

edges.relationship: Challenges a specific Marxist/Jacobin historiography of the French Revolution for reproducing revolutionary and commemorative categories.
edges.evidence_note: Primary pp. 255–256 read. Furet’s polemical label and diagnosis remain his claims about a specific historiographical dispute, not a critique of every Marxist or a personal arrow to Marx.

edges.relationship: Examines political language and claims to represent the people as mechanisms of revolutionary power.
edges.evidence_note: Named reader Gérard Grunberg, pp. 895 and 897, on Penser. Full book unread; no universal acceptance, deterministic twentieth-century analogy or inference from institutional membership.
